questions.prompt: Which list contains the five Feline Grimace Scale Action Units?

options.text: Ear position, orbital tightening, muzzle tension, whisker change, and head position.
options.feedback: This is the best answer. These five facial categories were validated together as an acute-pain scoring instrument.

options.text: Appetite, litter use, sleep, play, and vocalisation.
options.feedback: These are useful baseline categories, but they are not the five facial Action Units in the validated scale.

options.text: Tail height, back arch, paw position, gait speed, and breathing rate.
options.feedback: Some may inform broader observation, but this list does not represent the validated facial tool taught in this Capture.

questions.prompt: What is the most important validation boundary of the Feline Grimace Scale here?

options.text: It was validated for acute pain with trained scorers, not chronic pain or proven owner-level diagnostic accuracy.
options.feedback: This is the best answer and preserves both the tool's real rigor and the limits of the population and pain context studied.

options.text: It was validated only for senior cats with chronic arthritis scored by their owners.
options.feedback: That reverses the evidence. The study focused on naturally occurring acute pain and trained observers.

options.text: It has no empirical validation and is included only as an owner folklore checklist.
options.feedback: The scale is empirically validated. The caution concerns scope, not whether the research exists.

questions.prompt: Which is an owner-observable dental warning pattern?

options.text: Changed breath, drooling, face pawing, eating difficulty, gum change, or tooth loss.
options.feedback: This is the best answer. These observations can prompt assessment even when the cat has not completely stopped eating.

options.text: Only a visibly broken tooth or total refusal of every meal.
options.feedback: Dental disease can be much subtler. Waiting for a dramatic endpoint repeats the misconception this chapter addresses.

options.text: An owner-assigned diagnosis based on briefly lifting the lip at home.
options.feedback: Observation can identify warning signs, but definitive diagnosis requires anesthesia, probing, charting, and full-mouth x-rays.

questions.prompt: Why are face and mouth observations added to Milo's existing log?

options.text: So persistence and combinations can be compared with her baseline without creating an unsustainable separate ritual.
options.feedback: This is the best answer. The shared log can reveal a quiet cluster across days and observers that memory alone may miss.

options.text: So the household can calculate a diagnostic pain score without consulting a veterinarian.
options.feedback: The owner role is descriptive. The validation does not give lay observers authority to diagnose or self-treat.

options.text: So one photographed facial sign can override every other piece of context.
options.feedback: The method depends on combination, persistence, and context rather than granting one image automatic priority.

questions.prompt: Milo has ten days of slower one-sided eating, changed breath, reduced grooming, and repeated facial tension. What is the best response?

options.text: Describe the combined pattern to the vet promptly without naming a diagnosis or starting treatment.
options.feedback: This is the best response because the persistent unexplained cluster is meaningful even without a known emergency signature.

options.text: Wait until she refuses food because finishing meals proves the present signs are minor.
options.feedback: Continued eating does not erase quieter pain or dental signs. Waiting for dramatic deterioration defeats early recognition.

options.text: Score the photographs and begin pain medicine if the result seems high.
options.feedback: The study used trained scorers, and medication remains veterinarian-led. The household should report, not diagnose and treat.

questions.prompt: A cat squints and flattens her ears only during a nail trim, then immediately returns to baseline. What should happen?

options.text: Treat two Action Units as proof of an acute emergency.
options.feedback: This over-reads a momentary, context-explained response and skips the baseline method's explanation and resolution steps.

options.text: Log the context and watch for recurrence outside it; no escalation is supported by this isolated resolved event.
options.feedback: This is the best answer. It keeps the signs meaningful while avoiding over-escalation when context explains the whole event.

options.text: Discard the Action Units entirely because they appeared during a harmless procedure.
options.feedback: One context-explained appearance does not invalidate a tool. It demonstrates why the tool must be used with context.

questions.prompt: Three housemates each record one quiet sign on different days. No one noticed the full pattern alone. What is the strongest conclusion?

options.text: Separate observers make the entries too inconsistent to combine.
options.feedback: A shared record can be especially valuable across observers when each entry is specific and dated; the pattern need not live in one memory.

options.text: Read the dated entries together, compare the cluster with baseline, and act on persistence without overstating the cause.
options.feedback: This is the best synthesis of shared logging, combined-signal reading, and the owner-level boundary.

options.text: Choose the most medically concerning sign and ignore the others so the decision remains simple.
options.feedback: Removing corroborating signals makes the judgement weaker. The combined pattern is the reason quiet changes become visible.
